content: Diabetes is the primary cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) globally. To mitigate diabetes-related complications, including kidney failure, strategies such as blood pressure management and glucose control are employed. However, there is insufficient evidence to define the optimal blood glucose target range for preventing kidney failure. This study aimed to assess the benefits and risks of intensive glycaemic control (defined as HbA1c < 7% or fasting glucose levels < 120 mg/dL) compared to standard glycaemic control (HbA1c ≥ 7% or fasting glucose levels ≥ 120 mg/dL) in preventing the onset and progression of kidney disease in adults with diabetes. The researchers conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis, searching databases and clinical trial registries up to March 31, 2017. They included randomized controlled trials involving individuals aged 14 years or older with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, with or without pre-existing kidney disease. Participants were randomly assigned to either tight glucose control or less stringent glucose targets. The outcomes assessed included mortality, cardiovascular complications, doubling of serum creatinine (SCr), ESKD, and proteinuria. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system, and statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model. Fourteen studies involving 29,319 participants were included, with 11 studies (29,141 participants) contributing to the meta-analyses. The average treatment duration was approximately 57 months, ranging from 6 months to 10 years. The studies included participants with varying levels of kidney function. However, incomplete reporting of key methodological details led to uncertain risks of bias in many studies. The GRADE assessment indicated moderate confidence in the evidence for outcomes such as ESKD, all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, and progressive proteinuria, but low or very low confidence in the evidence for cardiovascular mortality and doubling of SCr. For the primary outcomes, intensive glycaemic control appeared to have little or no effect on the risk of doubling SCr (4 studies, 26,874 participants: RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.11; low certainty evidence), development of ESKD (4 studies, 23,332 participants: RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.12; low certainty evidence), all-cause mortality (9 studies, 29,094 participants: RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.13; moderate certainty evidence), cardiovascular mortality (6 studies, 23,673 participants: RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.92; low certainty evidence), or sudden death (4 studies, 5,913 participants: RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.26 to 2.57; very low certainty evidence). However, individuals receiving intensive glycaemic control likely experienced reduced risks of non-fatal myocardial infarction (5 studies, 25,596 participants: RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.99; moderate certainty evidence), onset of microalbuminuria (4 studies, 19,846 participants: RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.93; moderate certainty evidence), and progression of microalbuminuria (5 studies, 13,266 participants: RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.93; moderate certainty evidence). In absolute terms, intensive glucose control in 1,000 adults would prevent 0 to 2 cases of non-fatal myocardial infarction, 7 cases of new-onset albuminuria, and 2 cases of worsening albuminuria. The authors concluded that intensive glycaemic control in diabetes management resulted in similar risks of kidney failure, death, and major cardiovascular events compared to standard glucose control. However, it provided modest clinical benefits in reducing the onset and progression of microalbuminuria and non-fatal myocardial infarction. The adverse effects of intensive glycaemic management remain uncertain. The clinical significance of targeting an HbA1c < 7% or blood glucose < 6.6 mmol/L is unclear, and the potential harms of this approach are largely unmeasured.
